# Discrete Spin Structures and the Dimer Model on Surfaces with Boundary

## Background and Motivation

In earlier work, the authors established a fundamental correspondence between combinatorial and geometric structures on graphs embedded in surfaces. Specifically, they demonstrated that certain edge orientations of a graph $G$ embedded in a closed oriented surface $S$ admit a natural interpretation as discrete spin structures on that surface. This identification is not merely formal: it provides a genuinely geometric lens through which to view the combinatorics of edge orientations, revealing that the seemingly ad hoc orientation conditions used in dimer model computations actually encode topological information about spin structures on the underlying surface.

This correspondence proved to be more than a structural curiosity—it served as the foundation for a geometric proof of the celebrated Pfaffian formula for the partition function of the dimer model on $G$. Rather than relying on the classical, more algebraic derivation of this formula, the authors were able to reconstruct it through the topology of spin structures, thereby illuminating the deeper geometric mechanisms underlying the Kasteleyn theory of dimer coverings and providing a conceptual explanation for why the Pfaffian, rather than the determinant, naturally arises in this context.

## Extension to Surfaces with Boundary

The present article extends this circle of ideas to the more general and technically demanding setting of **compact oriented surfaces with boundary**. This generalization significantly broadens the scope of the original framework, since surfaces with boundary arise naturally both in topological considerations (e.g., when decomposing a closed surface via cutting) and in physical applications where boundary conditions play an essential role. Adapting the theory of discrete spin structures to this setting requires careful treatment of how edge orientations behave near and along the boundary components, and how the resulting spin structures should be understood in this more general topological context.

## Cutting, Gluing, and Their Effects on the Partition Function

A central theme of the paper is the systematic study of how **cutting and gluing operations** on the surface interact with the discrete spin structures defined by edge orientations. When a surface is cut along a curve, or when two boundary components are glued together, the associated combinatorial data—namely, the edge orientations of the embedded graph—must be tracked and modified accordingly. The paper analyzes precisely how these topological operations affect the underlying discrete spin structure, and consequently, how they transform the partition function of the dimer model.

This analysis is significant because it shows that the partition function is not merely a static invariant of the graph and its embedding, but rather transforms in a controlled and predictable way under surface decomposition. Understanding this transformation behavior is essential both for computational purposes—since it allows large or complex surfaces to be built up from simpler pieces—and for revealing the deeper structural properties of the dimer model.

## Toward a Quantum Field Theoretic Formulation

Perhaps the most far-reaching consequence of this cutting-and-gluing analysis is that it enables a **reformulation of the dimer model as a quantum field theory** defined on surface graphs. The ability to cut and glue surfaces while tracking the corresponding changes in the partition function mirrors precisely the gluing axioms that characterize topological and quantum field theories, in the spirit of the Atiyah-Segal axiomatic framework. By establishing this correspondence, the paper positions the dimer model within a broader field-theoretic context, opening the door to techniques and perspectives from quantum field theory to be applied to the combinatorial and statistical mechanical study of dimer coverings, and conversely, suggesting that the dimer model may serve as a concrete, combinatorially tractable model for exploring more general field-theoretic constructions on surfaces.

# Discrete Spin Structures and the Dimer Model on Surfaces with Boundary: A Quantum Field Theoretic Perspective

## Introduction

The dimer model, a fundamental object in combinatorial statistical mechanics, has long been understood to connect deeply with the theory of spin structures on surfaces. The celebrated Kasteleyn approach demonstrates that the partition function of the dimer model on a graph embedded in a surface can be computed as a signed sum of Pfaffians, with each sign choice corresponding to a discrete spin structure on the underlying surface. This correspondence has been thoroughly developed for closed surfaces, where the topological invariants of spin structures directly control the combinatorics of Kasteleyn orientations.

In this paper, we extend this framework to compact oriented surfaces with boundary. This generalization is not merely a technical extension but opens the door to a richer structural understanding of the dimer model, one that reveals its compatibility with the operations of cutting and gluing surfaces along their boundaries. Such compatibility is essential if one wishes to view the dimer model through the lens of quantum field theory, where the fundamental principle is that the theory should be constructible from local data via a gluing or sewing procedure—precisely the structure encoded by a functor from a suitable cobordism category to a category of vector spaces or algebras.

## Discrete Spin Structures on Surfaces with Boundary

We begin by developing the theory of discrete spin structures on compact oriented surfaces with boundary, building on the combinatorial formulation pioneered by Cimasoni and Reshetikhin, and further developed in related contexts by Kenyon, Cimasoni, and others. A discrete spin structure is defined combinatorially in terms of a choice of edges on a graph embedded in the surface satisfying certain local and global compatibility conditions, mirroring the topological definition of a spin structure as a lift of the frame bundle or, in dimension two, as a certain cohomological refinement of the mod-2 intersection pairing.

For closed surfaces, the space of discrete spin structures is a torsor over $H^1(\Sigma, \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$, and the Arf invariant of the spin structure controls the sign in the Pfaffian formula for the dimer partition function. When boundary is introduced, several new subtleties arise. First, one must specify appropriate boundary conditions for the discrete spin structure, analogous to the choice of Neveu-Schwarz or Ramond boundary conditions in the continuum theory of spin structures on Riemann surfaces with boundary. Second, the relative homology and cohomology groups $H^1(\Sigma, \partial \Sigma; \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^1(\Sigma; \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ both play a role in classifying the possible discrete spin structures, and one must carefully track how these structures behave under the operation of gluing two boundary circles together.

We show that the discrete spin structures on a surface with boundary, equipped with appropriate boundary data, form a torsor over $H^1(\Sigma, \partial\Sigma; \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$, and we establish an explicit combinatorial procedure for computing how the Arf invariant (or its natural analogue when boundary is present) transforms under cutting the surface along an embedded arc or circle, and correspondingly how it transforms under the reverse operation of gluing two boundary components.

## The Pfaffian Formula for the Dimer Partition Function on Surfaces with Boundary

Having established the discrete spin structure formalism, we turn to the dimer model itself. We formulate the dimer model on a graph $\Gamma$ embedded in a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$ with boundary, and derive a Pfaffian formula for the partition function as a signed sum over the set of discrete spin structures with prescribed boundary conditions, extending the Kasteleyn-Cimasoni-Reshetikhin formula:
$$
Z(\Gamma) = \sum_{\mathfrak{s}} (-1)^{\mathrm{Arf}(\mathfrak{s})} \mathrm{Pf}(K_\mathfrak{s})
$$
Here the sum ranges over the (now larger, boundary-dependent) set of discrete spin structures on $\Sigma$, and $K_\mathfrak{s}$ denotes the Kasteleyn matrix associated to the Kasteleyn orientation determined by $\mathfrak{s}$.

A key technical point in this generalization concerns the boundary conditions imposed on the graph $\Gamma$ itself: dimer configurations on a surface with boundary may leave certain boundary vertices unmatched, which corresponds to the introduction of monomer defects along the boundary, or alternatively, one can consider the dimer model with wired or free boundary conditions in analogy with the Ising model. We carefully analyze both cases and show that the Pfaffian formula persists with the sign structure suitably modified to account for the boundary data.

## Cutting and Gluing Operations

The heart of this paper lies in the analysis of how the discrete spin structures, the Kasteleyn orientations, and consequently the partition function itself transform under cutting and gluing operations on the surface. Specifically, we consider two basic operations:

1. **Cutting**: Given a surface $\Sigma$ and an embedded arc or circle $\gamma$, we cut $\Sigma$ along $\gamma$ to produce a new surface $\Sigma'$ (possibly disconnected) with additional boundary components corresponding to the two sides of $\gamma$.

2. **Gluing**: Conversely, given a surface $\Sigma$ with two boundary components (or two arcs on the boundary) $\partial_1, \partial_2$, we may glue these together via an orientation-reversing homeomorphism to produce a new surface $\hat{\Sigma}$.

We prove that discrete spin structures on $\Sigma$ correspond bijectively to discrete spin structures on $\Sigma'$ (respectively $\hat\Sigma$) satisfying compatible boundary conditions on the newly created (respectively identified) boundary components. Moreover, we show that the Kasteleyn orientation and the associated sign $(-1)^{\mathrm{Arf}(\mathfrak{s})}$ transform in a controlled, local way: cutting/gluing affects the global sign only through a computable correction term depending on the local combinatorics near the cut/gluing locus and the relative homological data of the spin structures involved.

This result allows us to express the partition function of the dimer model on a glued surface $\hat\Sigma$ in terms of data associated to the pieces before gluing, specifically as a bilinear pairing between "boundary states"—vectors in a vector space associated to each boundary circle, built from the dimer model's Kasteleyn/Pfaffian data restricted to the boundary. This is the key structural fact that permits the reformulation of the dimer model as a quantum field theory.

## The Dimer Model as a Quantum Field Theory on Surface Graphs

Building on the cutting and gluing formalism above, we construct a functorial assignment of algebraic data to surface graphs, in the spirit of topological quantum field theory (TQFT) as formalized by Atiyah and Segal, but adapted to the combinatorial and discrete setting appropriate for the dimer model. Concretely, to each boundary circle (or boundary arc with appropriate marked points) of a graph embedded in a surface, we associate a vector space—built from the Clifford algebra or fermionic Fock space generated by the boundary degrees of freedom of the dimer model, consistent with the discrete spin structure boundary conditions. To each surface graph with boundary, we associate a vector (or more generally, an element of the appropriate Fock space, or a state) determined by the dimer model's Kasteleyn/Pfaffian data.

We show that this assignment is compatible with the gluing operation: the state associated to a glued surface graph $\hat\Sigma$ is obtained from the states associated to the pieces by a natural contraction/pairing operation, mirroring the operadic composition rules of a quantum field theory. In particular, this allows the partition function of the dimer model on a large or complicated surface to be computed by decomposing the surface into simple pieces (such as pairs of pants, disks, or annuli), computing the corresponding quantum states on each piece, and then gluing these states together using the fermionic pairing.

This construction places the dimer model within a broader family of exactly solvable statistical mechanical models—including the Ising model—that admit a description as free-fermionic quantum field theories on surfaces. It offers a novel combinatorial approach to understanding the fermionic path integral formulation of the Ising/dimer correspondence, and provides new tools for understanding conformal field theory limits of the dimer model on surfaces with boundary, particularly relevant to the study of boundary conformal field theory and the role of spin structures in string theory compactifications and topological recursion.

## Organization and Outlook

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review the necessary background on discrete spin structures and the dimer model's Pfaffian formula for closed surfaces. We then develop the theory of discrete spin structures with boundary conditions, establishing the torsor structure and the transformation rules under cutting and gluing. We subsequently derive the boundary Pfaffian formula for the dimer partition function and analyze monomer/dimer boundary conditions. Finally, we construct the quantum field theoretic functor from surface graphs to vector spaces, verify the gluing axioms, and discuss examples including the disk, annulus, and pair of pants, illustrating explicitly how the partition function of the dimer model on more complex surfaces can be reconstructed from these elementary building blocks.

We conclude with a discussion of open questions, including the extension of this framework to non-orientable surfaces, the relationship to the Temperley bijection between dimers and spanning trees in the presence of boundary, and potential applications to the study of double-dimer models and their relationship to the Gaussian free field and $SLE_4$ processes on surfaces with boundary.

# Der Pfaffian: Eine mathematische Größe zwischen Determinante und Algebra

## Einführung

In der linearen Algebra begegnet man neben der bekannten Determinante einer weiteren, weniger geläufigen, aber äußerst faszinierenden Größe: dem **Pfaffian**. Benannt nach dem deutschen Mathematiker Johann Friedrich Pfaff, stellt der Pfaffian eine algebraische Invariante dar, die speziell für schiefsymmetrische Matrizen gerader Dimension definiert ist.

## Die zentrale These

Die zentrale **These** dieser Betrachtung lautet: Der Pfaffian ist nicht bloß eine Rechenvorschrift, sondern verkörpert eine tiefere strukturelle Wahrheit über die Geometrie schiefsymmetrischer Formen. Diese These lässt sich anhand mehrerer mathematischer Zusammenhänge belegen.

## Mathematische Grundlagen

Für eine schiefsymmetrische Matrix A der Größe 2n × 2n gilt die bemerkenswerte Beziehung:

$$\det(A) = \text{Pf}(A)^2$$

Diese Formel offenbart bereits die erste wichtige Eigenschaft: Der Pfaffian ist gewissermaßen die „Quadratwurzel" der Determinante – jedoch mit dem entscheidenden Unterschied, dass er als Polynom in den Matrixeinträgen definiert ist und somit auch das Vorzeichen korrekt erfasst, welches bei der bloßen Quadratwurzel der Determinante verloren ginge.

## Anwendungsbereiche

Der Pfaffian findet in zahlreichen Gebieten Anwendung:

- **Theoretische Physik**: insbesondere in der Quantenfeldtheorie bei der Berechnung von Fermion-Determinanten
- **Kombinatorik**: bei der Abzählung perfekter Matchings in Graphen
- **Differentialgeometrie**: im Zusammenhang mit der Krümmung von Mannigfaltigkeiten
- **Algebraische Geometrie**: bei der Untersuchung spezieller Varietäten

## Schlussfolgerung

Die eingangs formulierte These, dass der Pfaffian tiefere strukturelle Zusammenhänge widerspiegelt als eine reine Rechengröße, bestätigt sich durch seine vielfältigen Anwendungen und seine enge Verbindung zur Determinantentheorie. Der Pfaffian bleibt somit ein Paradebeispiel dafür, wie scheinbar abstrakte mathematische Konzepte praktische Relevanz in unterschiedlichsten wissenschaftlichen Disziplinen entfalten können.

We extend the theory of discrete spin structures and dimer models, previously developed for closed surfaces, to the setting of surfaces with boundary. A discrete spin structure is encoded combinatorially via a Kasteleyn orientation on a graph embedded in the surface, and we show how such structures behave naturally under the presence of boundary components, extending the correspondence between Kasteleyn orientations and (relative) spin structures to this more general context. We introduce and study cutting and gluing operations on dimer models and their associated discrete spin structures, showing that these operations are compatible with the topological cutting and gluing of surfaces along embedded curves and boundary components. In particular, we characterize how Kasteleyn orientations transform under such surgery operations, and how the partition function of the dimer model changes accordingly, generalizing the multiplicative and gluing formulas known from the closed case.

Building on this combinatorial framework, we reformulate the dimer model on surfaces with boundary as a topological quantum field theory (TQFT)-like structure, in which surfaces with boundary are assigned vector spaces (built from sums over discrete spin structures or from fermionic Fock spaces) and dimer partition functions arise as pairings or amplitudes associated to cobordisms. We show that the cutting/gluing formulas correspond precisely to the composition axioms of this TQFT reformulation, providing a functorial description of the dimer model compatible with gluing along boundaries. This perspective clarifies the role of spin structures as a necessary decoration for the theory to behave functorially under cutting and gluing, and it opens the way to relate discrete dimer TQFTs with their continuum analogues, such as the Ising model and free fermion conformal field theories, on surfaces with boundary.

# Abstract

The dimer model on graphs embedded in closed oriented surfaces admits an elegant description of the partition function as an alternating sum of Pfaffians, indexed by elements of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{2g}$, corresponding to the $2^{2g}$ Kasteleyn orientations determined by the choice of spin structure on the genus $g$ surface. In this paper, we extend this framework to graphs embedded in compact oriented surfaces with nonempty boundary. We show that the partition function of the dimer model on such a surface of genus $g$ with $b$ boundary components can be expressed as a signed sum of Pfaffians indexed by $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{2g+b-1}$, reflecting the enlarged first cohomology group of the surface relative to its boundary. The presence of boundary introduces new combinatorial and topological subtleties: Kasteleyn orientations are no longer uniquely determined up to the torus-type ambiguity of the closed case, and the relevant notion of discrete spin structure must be adapted to account for boundary components, each contributing an independent $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$-valued holonomy. We develop the necessary theory of discrete spin structures on ribbon graphs with boundary, prove a boundary-compatible version of the Kasteleyn sign condition, and establish the resulting Pfaffian formula via a careful analysis of the associated Arf-type invariant and its behavior under gluing. As applications, we discuss compatibility with cut-and-glue operations along boundary components, relations to open dimer models and boundary monodromy, and connections to the enumeration of spanning trees and the Ising model on surfaces with boundary. We illustrate our results with explicit examples on the disk, annulus, and pair of pants, and discuss implications for the asymptotic and conformal-limit behavior of the model in the presence of boundary conditions.

In this paper, we extend this framework to graphs embedded in surfaces with boundary. We prove a gluing formula expressing the Pfaffian of the glued graph in terms of the Pfaffians of the pieces together with an explicit transition term depending on the choice of orientation and spin structure compatibility along the gluing curve. # Summary

This paper extends the established correspondence between spin structures, dimer models, and Pfaffian formulas from closed surfaces to the more general setting of **bordered surfaces** (surfaces with boundary). Building on prior work that established how Kasteleyn orientations encode spin structures on closed Riemann surfaces—allowing partition functions of the dimer model to be expressed as linear combinations of Pfaffians indexed by spin structures—the present work develops the analogous formalism when the underlying surface has boundary components.

The central technical contribution is a **cut-and-glue** framework: bordered surfaces are decomposed into elementary pieces along boundary circles, and the spin-Pfaffian correspondence is analyzed under this decomposition. The paper shows how Kasteleyn orientations, discrete spin structures, and their associated Pfaffians behave consistently under cutting a surface along a curve and regluing, establishing gluing/factorization rules that mirror the operator-theoretic composition rules of a **topological quantum field theory (TQFT)**. Boundary conditions on the dimer/Ising degrees of freedom are shown to correspond naturally to the choice of vector spaces (Hilbert spaces) assigned to boundary circles, while the bulk partition function corresponds to the TQFT-type "propagator" or amplitude assigned to the cobordism.

The authors verify consistency of this construction under composition of cobordisms, and discuss how known results for closed surfaces (expressing the full dimer partition function as a signed sum of Pfaffians over spin structures) are recovered as a special "closing off" of the boundary.

The paper thus provides a rigorous bridge between the combinatorial dimer/Ising-Pfaffian technology and a categorical/quantum-field-theoretic language, opening a route to systematically compute and organize partition functions on surfaces of arbitrary genus and boundary via cutting-and-gluing, analogous to techniques used in conformal field theory and TQFT.
